title: The governor: fuel, speed and droop

interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is the trace dip as the flywheel slows, then climb back as the fuel rises, settling lower on its droop line, when you tap a load step.
interactive.title: The droop line
interactive.whatAmILookingAt:
Thirteen small screens on one picture, with Back and Continue. Five show an idea and eight ask you to try it. No marks and no timers.

The picture. On the left, a generator set drawn side-on along one shaft: an engine, a flywheel and the alternator, each labelled. A fuel bar beside the engine shows the fuel as a percentage of full-load fuel. A mark on the flywheel shows it turn faster or slower. Two arrows on the shaft, drawn to scale, show the engine's torque driving forward and the alternator's pulling back. On the right, a graph of frequency, 56 to 66 Hz, against load, 0 to 504 kW. It shows the governor's line and a dot at the present load and frequency. Under it, a trace of frequency against time over the last 6 s, 54 to 72 Hz, with 60 Hz dashed. On a phone the three stack. The load stepper has five settings: 0%, 25%, 50%, 75% and 100% of 504 kW. It opens on 0%. Each tap moves the load one setting at once. A Trip button drops all the load at once. The droop slider runs 0% to 6% in steps of 1, opening at 4%. At 0% its label reads Isochronous. The set point slider runs 58.0 to 64.0 Hz in steps of 0.1, opening at 62.4 Hz.

The readouts, in four tiles that wrap onto two rows on a phone: Load in kW, Fuel in %, Speed in rev/min and Frequency in Hz. The stepper's five settings and the Trip button wrap too, so no word splits.

The rule it computes. The set has 4 poles and is rated 504 kW at 1800 rev/min, 60 Hz. Frequency is pole pairs × rev/min ÷ 60, so rev/min = 30 × the frequency. Its speed in rad/s is rev/min × 2π ÷ 60, 188.5 rad/s at 1800 rev/min. The shaft carries 20 kg m² of inertia. The load takes its kW whatever the speed. The engine's power is the fuel % × 504 kW. Each torque is its power ÷ the speed in rad/s. The speed changes at (engine torque − load torque) ÷ 20 kg m², in rad/s². The governor measures the frequency. Its target is the set point − droop % × 60 Hz ÷ 100 × fuel % ÷ 100. So with 4% droop and a 62.4 Hz set point, the target is 62.4 Hz at no fuel and 60.0 Hz at full fuel. At 0% droop the target is the set point at any fuel. The governor's fuel demand is 12% for each hertz the frequency sits below its target, plus a running total that grows by 12% a second for each hertz below. The total stops growing while the demand sits at a limit. The fuel follows the demand after a 0.1 s wait, closing the gap with a time constant of 0.1 s. It runs from 0% to 110%. When the governor asks for less than nothing, the bar sits at 0% and the engine's own friction drags the shaft, by up to 10% of 504 kW. At a steady speed the engine's power equals the load's, so the fuel % equals the load %. So the dot settles on its line: frequency = set point − droop % × 60 ÷ 100 × load ÷ 504 kW. During a step the dot falls below the line, then climbs back to it. Time runs three times slower than real.

Screen 1, try it, a recall. No picture. "A flywheel of 2 kg m² feels 50 N m of net torque. How fast does its speed rise?" A field in rad/s². Answer 25 rad/s². Slips: 100, "That multiplies. The speed changes at net torque ÷ inertia."; 0.04, "That is upside down. The torque goes on top." Hint when wrong: "Net torque = inertia × angular acceleration. Rearrange for the acceleration." Why: "Angular acceleration = net torque ÷ inertia = 50 ÷ 2 = 25 rad/s². It keeps rising at that rate for as long as the torques stay unbalanced." A right Check says "Still there." Read: the question.

Screen 2, show. Droop at 0%, the set point at 60.0 Hz, the load at 25%, steady. The sliders and stepper are hidden. The words: "A set on its own makes whatever power its load draws. The alternator pulls back on the shaft with a torque, power ÷ speed. The engine drives it forward. While the two torques match, the speed holds. Any gap goes into or out of the spinning mass, as on a flywheel. The governor keeps them matched. It measures the speed, compares it with its set point and moves the fuel. It is the AVR's loop again, with fuel in place of field." Read: the words. Still: the load at 25%, the two torque arrows equal, 126 kW, 25%, 1800 rev/min and 60.0 Hz.

Screen 3, try it, a prediction. Droop at 0%, the set point at 60.0 Hz, the load at 0%, steady at 60.0 Hz. "The set runs alone at 60 Hz with no load. A load of 25% lands all at once. The governor is working. What does the frequency do?" Three choices, in this order: "It holds at 60 Hz, because the governor adds fuel at once"; "It dips first, then climbs back as the fuel rises"; "It rises, because the governor adds fuel". Right, the second. Hint for the first: "This governor measures the speed, so it adds fuel only once the speed starts to fall. The engine then takes time to answer." Hint for the third: "The load pulls back on the shaft before any extra fuel arrives. So the speed falls first." Why: "The load's torque arrives at once. The fuel takes time to follow. Until it does, the gap slows the spinning mass, so the frequency dips. Then the fuel catches up and the speed climbs back." A right Check plays the step: the load goes to 25%, the trace dips, then climbs back. Read: the question.

Screen 4, show. Droop at 0%, the set point at 60.0 Hz, the load at 0%, steady. The stepper is free. The words: "Tap the load up to 25%, 126 kW. At 1800 rev/min, 188.5 rad/s, the load's torque rises by 126 000 ÷ 188.5 = 668 N m at once. The fuel has not moved yet. So the load's arrow outgrows the engine's, the flywheel slows and the trace dips. This fall is a frequency dip.[^3] After 0.1 s the fuel bar starts to rise. The gap closes and the speed climbs back." Read: "Adding 126 kW at 188.5 rad/s raises the load's torque by 668 N m at once. The fuel has not moved yet, so the flywheel slows and the frequency dips. Then the fuel rises and the speed climbs back." Still: the load at 25% after the step has played, the trace showing the dip and the climb back, 126 kW, 25%, 1800 rev/min and 60.0 Hz.

Screen 5, try it, typed. Droop at 0%, the set point at 60.0 Hz, the load at 0%. "The load's torque has jumped by 668 N m. The fuel has not moved yet. The shaft carries 20 kg m². How fast does the set slow?" A field in rad/s². Answer 33.4 rad/s². Slips: 13 360, "That multiplies. The speed changes at torque ÷ inertia."; 0.03, "That is upside down. The torque goes on top."; 6.3, "That divides the 126 kW. Use the torque gap, 668 N m." Hint when wrong: "It is the flywheel sum from the first screen." Why: "668 ÷ 20 = 33.4 rad/s². In the 0.1 s before the fuel moves, the set loses 33.4 × 0.1 = 3.34 rad/s. That is 1.8% of 188.5 rad/s. The frequency follows the speed, so it falls 1.8% too, from 60 to 58.9 Hz." A right Check plays the step and marks 58.9 Hz on the trace at 0.1 s. Read: the question.

Screen 6, show. Droop at 0%, the set point at 60.0 Hz, the load at 25%, steady after its step. The stepper is free. The words: "Look where the speed came back to: exactly 60.0 Hz. The governor kept adding fuel until the frequency was back at its set point. The fuel now matches the load, 25%. Tap the load up again. Each step dips the trace, and each time it climbs back to 60 Hz. On the graph the dot slides along a flat line. A governor that holds the same speed at any load is called isochronous." Read: "The governor kept adding fuel until the frequency was back at its set point, 60.0 Hz. The fuel now matches the load. At every load the dot returns to the same flat line. A governor that holds the same speed at any load is called isochronous." Still: the load at 75%, three dips on the trace, each back to 60 Hz, 378 kW, 75%, 1800 rev/min and 60.0 Hz.

Screen 7, try it. Droop at 0%, the set point at 60.0 Hz, the load at 50%, steady. "An isochronous set runs at 60 Hz with 50% load. The load steps up to 75%. Once it settles, what has changed?" Three choices, in this order: "The fuel, now higher to match the bigger load"; "The frequency, now a little lower"; "Nothing, fuel and frequency are back where they were". Right, the first. Hint for the second: "An isochronous governor keeps adding fuel until the speed is back at its set point." Hint for the third: "The load is bigger, so the engine must make more power to hold the speed." Why: "Holding the speed needs the engine's torque to match the load's. A bigger load needs more torque, so more fuel. The governor brings the frequency back to 60 Hz, and the fuel settles at 75%." A right Check plays the step: the trace dips and returns to 60 Hz, and the fuel bar settles at 75%. Read: the question.

Screen 8, show. Droop at 0%, the set point at 62.4 Hz, the load at 0%, steady. The droop slider and the stepper are free. The words: "Drag the droop to 4%. The line tilts down from 62.4 Hz. The governor now lets the speed settle lower as the load grows. Droop is the change in speed, as a percentage, that takes the governor through its full travel.[^1] With 5% droop, full load runs at 100% speed and no load at 105%.[^2] Here 4% of 60 Hz is 2.4 Hz. So no load sits at 62.4 Hz and full load at 60 Hz. Step the load up and the dot walks down its line." Read: "With 4% droop the line tilts down from 62.4 Hz at no load to 60 Hz at full load. Droop is the change in speed, as a percentage, that takes the governor through its full travel. 4% of 60 Hz is 2.4 Hz. As the load steps up, the dot walks down its line." Still: droop at 4%, the load at 100%, the readouts at 504 kW, 100%, 1800 rev/min and 60.0 Hz.

Screen 9, try it, typed. Droop at 4%, the set point at 62.4 Hz, the load at 0%, the Frequency tile reading ? until Check. "With 4% droop, this set runs at 62.4 Hz with no load and 60 Hz at full load, 504 kW. What frequency does it settle at with 252 kW?" A field in Hz. Answer 61.2 Hz. Slips: 60, "60 Hz is full load. At half load the line has fallen only half its 2.4 Hz."; 60.4, "That takes the droop as 4 Hz. 4% of 60 Hz is 2.4 Hz."; 63.6, "The frequency falls as the load grows. Take the fall off." Hint when wrong: "252 kW is half of 504 kW. So the line has fallen half its 2.4 Hz." Why: "252 ÷ 504 = 0.5. The line falls 2.4 Hz from no load to full load, so half load falls 1.2 Hz. 62.4 − 1.2 = 61.2 Hz." A right Check steps the load to 50%, and the dot settles at 61.2 Hz. Read: the question.

Screen 10, show. Droop at 4%, the set point at 62.4 Hz, the load at 50%, steady at 61.2 Hz. The set point slider and the Trip button are free. The words: "The set point lifts the whole line without tilting it. Drag it, and the dot rides up or down with it at the same load. So the set point picks the load at which the set runs at 60 Hz. Droop has a cost on a set alone: its frequency moves with its load. Tap Trip. The trace overshoots, then the dot settles at the top of its line, 62.4 Hz, above 60 Hz." Read: "The set point lifts the whole line without tilting it, so it picks the load at which the set runs at 60 Hz. When all the load trips, the trace overshoots, then the dot settles at the top of its line, 62.4 Hz, above 60 Hz." Still: the set point at 62.4 Hz, after the trip, the load at 0%, the overshoot on the trace, 0 kW, 0%, 1872 rev/min and 62.4 Hz.

Screen 11, try it, typed. Droop at 4%, the set point at 62.4 Hz, the load at 75%, steady at 60.6 Hz, the set point slider hidden. "With 4% droop, you want this set at exactly 60 Hz with 378 kW, 75% of its rating. What set point, its no-load frequency, do you choose?" A field in Hz. Answer 61.8 Hz. Slips: 62.4, "That gives 60 Hz at full load. At 75% the line has fallen less."; 58.2, "The set point is the top of the line. It sits above 60 Hz."; 63, "That takes the droop as 4 Hz. 4% of 60 Hz is 2.4 Hz." Hint when wrong: "Find how far the line falls by 75% load. Add that to 60 Hz." Why: "The full fall is 2.4 Hz. By 75% load the line has fallen 0.75 × 2.4 = 1.8 Hz. So its top must sit 1.8 Hz above 60 Hz, at 61.8 Hz." A right Check moves the set point to 61.8 Hz, and the dot rises to 60.0 Hz at 378 kW. Read: the question.

Screen 12, try it (mixed). Droop at 4%, the set point at 60.0 Hz, the load at 100%, steady at 57.6 Hz. "A set on 4% droop runs at 60.0 Hz with no load. On full load it settles at 57.6 Hz. Fault or design?" Three choices, in this order: "A fault: the governor cannot hold the speed"; "Design: droop working, with the set point too low"; "A fault: the engine is short of power". Right, the second. Hint for the first: "Work out the line. 4% of 60 Hz is 2.4 Hz below the no-load frequency." Hint for the third: "The set carries its full load and its speed is steady. The fall matches its droop exactly." Why: "4% of 60 Hz is 2.4 Hz. 60.0 − 2.4 = 57.6 Hz, exactly on its line. The governor is doing what it was set to do. Raise the set point to 62.4 Hz and full load lands on 60 Hz." A right Check drags the set point to 62.4 Hz, and the dot rises to 60.0 Hz. Read: the question.

Screen 13, try it, typed (mixed). No picture. "Another set makes 50 Hz. It has 5% droop and runs at 50 Hz on full load. All its load trips. What frequency does it settle at?" A field in Hz. Answer 52.5 Hz. Slips: 55, "That takes the droop as 5 Hz. 5% of 50 Hz is 2.5 Hz."; 47.5, "Losing load sends the dot up its line, not down."; 50, "That is isochronous. With droop the set settles at the top of its line." Hint when wrong: "5% of 50 Hz is the droop in hertz. A trip sends the set to the top of its line." Why: "5% of 50 Hz is 2.5 Hz. Full load sits at 50 Hz, so no load sits at 50 + 2.5 = 52.5 Hz. The frequency overshoots first, then settles there." A right Check shows a closing line: "The governor holds the speed with fuel. Droop sets how far it gives with load." Read: the question.
interactive.ignores: Time is slowed three times so you can follow it. The governor here waits a fixed 0.1 s, then moves the fuel smoothly. A real engine's answer depends on its fuel system, its turbocharger and its tuning, so real dips are deeper or shallower. A governor tuned too eagerly overshoots and swings about its speed, which is called hunting. Here it is tuned to settle cleanly. The engine's power is drawn in proportion to its fuel, with no losses at a steady load. The voltage is not drawn. A slower set also makes less voltage, so a frequency dip adds to the voltage dip until the AVR catches up. The load draws the same power whatever the speed.

explain.text:
The governor and the AVR are the two basic controls on every set.[^10] The AVR trims the field to hold the voltage. The governor trims the fuel to hold the speed, and so the frequency. A sudden load slows the set first, and the governor then adds fuel to catch it. Where the speed settles after that is a setting.

On its own, a set makes whatever power its load draws. The alternator pulls back on the shaft with a torque, power ÷ speed. The engine's torque must match it, or the gap speeds up or slows the spinning mass. Add 126 kW to a set turning at 1800 rev/min, which is 188.5 rad/s. The load's torque rises by 126 000 ÷ 188.5 = 668 N m at once. The fuel cannot follow at once, so for a moment the engine falls short. With 20 kg m² on the shaft, an example value, the set slows at 668 ÷ 20 = 33.4 rad/s². Say the governor takes 0.1 s to answer. By then the set has lost 3.34 rad/s, 1.8% of its speed. The frequency follows the speed, so it falls 1.8% too, from 60 to 58.9 Hz. This fall is a [[frequency dip]].[^3] The governor then adds fuel, the gap closes and the speed climbs back.

Where it climbs back to depends on the governor. Textbooks call a governor that brings the speed exactly back to its set point, at any load, [[isochronous]]. The other kind lowers its own target speed as it opens the fuel. More load needs more fuel, so the speed settles lower. That fall is its [[droop]]: the change in speed, as a percentage, that takes the governor through its full travel, from no load to full load.[^1] With 5% droop, full load runs at 100% of rated speed and no load at 105%.[^2] On a 60 Hz set with 4% droop, 4% of 60 Hz is 2.4 Hz. So no load runs at 62.4 Hz and full load at 60 Hz, with a straight line between. At half load, 252 kW of 504 kW, the set runs at 62.4 − 2.4 × 0.5 = 61.2 Hz. The set point slides the whole line up or down without tilting it.

Droop is set on purpose. When sets run side by side, speed control is what shares the kW between them.[^11] On a set alone, its cost is that the frequency moves with the load. If all the load trips, the set settles at the top of its line, above its rated frequency. These figures come from a simplified picture, with a fixed response time and example values for the inertia. **The governor trims the fuel to hold the speed: isochronous brings it back exactly, and droop lets it settle a set few per cent lower from no load to full load.**

analogy.text: Think of a battery with some internal resistance. Its terminal voltage is its open-circuit voltage minus the current × r, a straight line falling with load. The open-circuit voltage plays the set point, and r plays the droop. A regulated supply that holds its voltage at any current plays the isochronous governor. Put two cells in parallel, and their open-circuit voltages and slopes decide how they share the current.
analogy.breaks: A cell's slope is a real loss inside it, turned into heat. A governor's droop wastes nothing, because it is only a setting in the control. And a cell answers a load at once, while a set dips first, because its fuel must catch up with a spinning mass.

practice.text:
**Working out a droop line**

- Find the droop in hertz: the droop % × the rated frequency ÷ 100.
- If the set runs at its rated frequency on full load, its no-load frequency is the rated frequency plus the droop in hertz.
- At any load, the frequency is the no-load frequency − the droop in hertz × the load ÷ the rated load.
- To run at a chosen frequency at a chosen load, set the no-load set point to that frequency + the droop in hertz × the load ÷ the rated load.
- For a sudden load, find the torque gap: the kW added × 1000 ÷ the speed in rad/s. The set slows at that gap ÷ the inertia until the fuel catches up.

**Rules of thumb:** a sudden load dips the frequency before the governor can catch it. A set alone on droop runs high on light load. It sits at its rated frequency only at the load its set point was chosen for.

**Worked example:** a 50 Hz set rated 400 kW has 3% droop and runs at 50 Hz on full load. Its droop in hertz is 3 × 50 ÷ 100 = 1.5 Hz, so no load sits at 51.5 Hz. At 240 kW, 0.6 of its rating, it runs at 51.5 − 1.5 × 0.6 = 51.5 − 0.9 = 50.6 Hz. To run it at 50 Hz on 240 kW, set its no-load point to 50 + 0.9 = 50.9 Hz.

**Common mistakes**
- Treating droop as a fault. A set on droop that settles below its no-load frequency is doing what it was set to do.
- Taking the droop % as hertz. 4% of 60 Hz is 2.4 Hz, not 4 Hz.
- Expecting the governor to stop the dip. A governor that measures speed adds fuel only once the speed has started to fall, and the engine takes time to answer.
- Forgetting that a load trip sends a set on droop above its rated frequency.
